title: If You Had to Ship This in a Month, What Would You Cut?
summary: Tests whether you can separate must-have from nice-to-have under real deadline pressure and articulate the user-facing cost of each cut, rather than vaguely promising to move faster.

slides.markdown:
The interviewer asks: **"if you had to ship this in a month, what would you cut?"** "We'd just work harder or move faster" isn't a real answer to a scoping question — it dodges the actual skill being tested, which is separating must-have from nice-to-have under real pressure.

A strong answer names the core capability that must ship, then names specific pieces to cut or downgrade, each with its concrete user-facing cost.

Ask what the one thing is that this system absolutely cannot fail to do, even in a minimal version. Is the deadline truly fixed, or is there room to negotiate scope with the business first?

Both questions shape the whole answer: the first defines what can never be cut, and the second determines whether "cutting scope" is even the right frame versus "renegotiating the deadline" being on the table too.

Identify the core user-facing capability that must ship, and name specific pieces you'd cut or downgrade — each with the concrete cost of cutting it, not just "we'd simplify."

The phrase "we'd simplify" is a red flag on its own — it names no specific feature and no specific cost. The skeleton forces both: which feature, and what the user loses without it.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: scoping a ticket-booking system
slides.markdown:
A worked example: for a ticket-booking system, the core that must ship is "a user can search, select, and pay for a seat without double-booking it." Cut for launch: multi-currency support (ship USD-only), seat-map visualization (ship a simple list of available seats), and email receipts (ship an in-app confirmation only, add email post-launch).

Each cut is named specifically, with a concrete downgrade path — not "we'd simplify the UI" but exactly which feature becomes a plainer version, and which one is deferred entirely.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: the tempting wrong cut
slides.markdown:
A concrete scenario: the team is tempted to cut the double-booking prevention logic itself to save a week, since it's the hardest part to build correctly. That's the wrong cut, because it's the one thing that actually protects the business from real financial and reputational damage.

The discipline here is cutting *features*, never cutting the core correctness guarantee — even when the correctness guarantee happens to be the hardest and most tempting thing to defer under pressure.

![Two scoping paths from auto-scaling infra: cut entirely versus downgrade to a fixed instance](assets/deadline-scoping-paths.svg)

For something that can't be fully dropped, launch on a fixed, generously-sized instance and monitor manually instead of building auto-scaling infrastructure in month one, with auto-scaling as a fast-follow once real traffic patterns are known.

This is a third option beyond "ship it fully" or "cut it entirely" — a deliberately simpler version that still covers the requirement, just without the engineering investment a fully automated version would need.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
Cutting scope to hit a deadline trades completeness now for technical or product debt later — the fast-follow work actually has to happen. The real skill isn't cutting, it's cutting the *right* things and being explicit about what's deferred, not silently dropped.

A silently dropped feature tends to stay dropped forever, since no one owns bringing it back; an explicitly deferred one, tracked with intent, actually gets built.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: the business insists nothing can be cut
slides.markdown:
Follow-up: "the business insists nothing can be cut and the deadline can't move — what do you say?" Make the trade-off explicit and force the conversation: name what quality or scope will actually suffer if both constraints are held, rather than silently absorbing an impossible ask.

Silently absorbing it doesn't make the conflict go away — it just delays the moment it surfaces, usually as a worse outcome (a rushed, buggy launch) than if it had been named upfront.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: making sure deferred work actually gets built
slides.markdown:
Follow-up: "you shipped the cut-down version — how do you make sure the deferred pieces actually get built later and don't just get forgotten?" Track deferred scope as committed backlog items with an owner and rough timeline at launch time, not a vague "we'll get to it."

Deprioritized-forever is the default outcome for anything left as a vague intention rather than a tracked commitment made at the moment of cutting.

**Wrong move:** cutting the core correctness or safety guarantee to save time, rather than cutting peripheral features, because the core is usually the hardest and most tempting thing to defer.

**Why it's wrong:** the correctness guarantee is exactly what protects the business from real damage — a double-booked seat or an incorrect payment has direct financial and reputational cost that a missing seat-map visualization never would.

**Correct model:** cut features aggressively before ever touching the core correctness guarantee, even under severe time pressure.

Name the core user-facing capability that must ship, then name specific features to cut or downgrade, each with a concrete user-facing cost — never a vague "we'd simplify." Never cut the core correctness or safety guarantee itself; that's the one thing worth protecting even under real pressure.

Track every deferred piece as a committed backlog item with an owner, since a silently dropped feature tends to stay dropped. If the business insists nothing can be cut and the deadline can't move, force that conflict into the open rather than absorbing it silently.
